text: Central Rotokas, spoken on Bougainville in Papua New Guinea, uses only about 11 distinctive sounds. Taa, spoken in Botswana and Namibia, has by some counts over 100, many of them clicks. English has around 40.
Ubykh, a language of the Caucasus, had roughly 80 consonants but only two or three vowels. Its last fluent speaker, Tevfik Esenç, died in 1992.
Noam Chomsky's sentence 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' (1957) is grammatically flawless and completely meaningless: his demonstration that grammar works independently of sense.
'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo' is a grammatical English sentence. It means: bison from Buffalo, whom other Buffalo bison bully, themselves bully Buffalo bison.
'The horse raced past the barn fell' is a correct English sentence. Readers stumble because they take 'raced' as the main verb; it means 'the horse that was raced past the barn fell'.
Grimm's law explains why Latin pater, tres and centum line up with English father, three and hundred: early Germanic speakers shifted the old p to f, t to th and k to h.

Before the Great Vowel Shift of roughly 1400 to 1700, English 'bite' sounded much like modern 'beet'. Spelling never caught up, which is why English vowel letters differ from their values in most European languages.

In 1786 William Jones told the Asiatic Society in Calcutta that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin must have 'sprung from some common source, which, perhaps, no longer exists'. We now call it Proto-Indo-European.

The legend of hundreds of Eskimo words for snow grew from a 1911 remark by Franz Boas that listed four. Since Inuit and Yupik languages build long words from roots, counting 'words' for snow means little anyway.
The word 'mondegreen' comes from Sylvia Wright, who as a child heard the ballad line 'and laid him on the green' as 'and Lady Mondegreen'. She coined the term in Harper's Magazine in 1954.

Philosopher Paul Grice argued that conversation runs on unspoken rules: be informative, truthful, relevant and clear. That is why 'some of the students passed' suggests not all did, though it never says so.

In 1962 William Labov asked New York department store clerks questions whose answer was 'fourth floor'. Staff at upscale Saks pronounced the r's far more often than staff at the bargain store S. Klein.
The quip 'A language is a dialect with an army and navy' was published by the Yiddish linguist Max Weinreich in 1945. He credited it to a listener who came up to him after one of his lectures.
English has essentially one productive infix, and it is rude: 'abso-bloody-lutely'. It must go right before the stressed syllable, so 'fan-bloody-tastic' works and 'fanta-bloody-stic' does not.
In a 2001 study by V. S. Ramachandran and Edward Hubbard, about 95% of people named a rounded blob 'bouba' and a spiky shape 'kiki'. Wolfgang Köhler had found a similar effect in 1929.
On La Gomera in the Canary Islands, Silbo Gomero renders Spanish as whistles that carry for kilometers across ravines. UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage in 2009, and island schools teach it.
'Nice' comes from Latin nescius, 'ignorant'. In medieval English it meant foolish or silly, and only after centuries of drift did it come to mean pleasant.
An adder was once 'a nadder' and an apron 'a napron': the n slid over to the article. 'Nickname' went the other way, from 'an ekename', meaning an additional name.

Benjamin Whorf claimed the Hopi language had no words or grammar referring to time. In 1983 the linguist Ekkehart Malotki published a study of some 600 pages documenting Hopi tenses, time units and temporal expressions.

When Nicaragua opened a school for deaf children in Managua in 1977, teachers taught only lip-reading. The children built a new sign language among themselves, and each younger cohort made its grammar richer.
Object-verb-subject is among the rarest basic word orders. In Hixkaryana, spoken in the Brazilian Amazon, it is the normal order, as if English said 'man ate jaguar' for 'the jaguar ate the man'.

'Lion-Eating Poet in the Stone Den', published by Yuen Ren Chao, is a Classical Chinese poem of over 90 characters, all pronounced shi in Mandarin with only the tones differing. Read aloud, it is gibberish.

'Ghoti' for 'fish' is usually pinned on George Bernard Shaw, but it appears nowhere in his writings; the earliest known example is an 1855 letter. It fails anyway: 'gh' never says f at the start of an English word.
Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr in northern Australia describe locations by compass direction rather than by left and right. Instead of 'move to your left' they might say 'move a bit to the east'.

Using 'literally' as a mere intensifier is not a modern decline. The Oxford English Dictionary's earliest example of the figurative sense comes from Frances Brooke's 1769 novel The History of Emily Montague.

In their 1969 survey, Brent Berlin and Paul Kay proposed that languages gain color words in a set order. A language with only three basic color terms has black, white and red; green or yellow comes next.

Germanic languages lost the old Indo-European word for bear, still seen in Greek arktos and Latin ursus. English 'bear' probably meant 'the brown one', perhaps a way to avoid naming a dangerous animal.

Daniel Everett argued in 2005 that the Amazonian language Pirahã lacks embedded clauses, challenging the idea that recursion is universal in human language. Other linguists dispute his analysis; the debate continues.
In the Australian language Mbabaram, the word for dog is dog. The match with English is pure coincidence: regular sound changes turned an older local word, gudaga, into dúg.

Hebrew is the best-known language to regain native speakers after centuries with none. Itamar Ben-Avi, born in Jerusalem in 1882 to the reviver Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, is usually called its first modern native speaker.
